passages.title: Ar-Rahman teaches the Quran and speech
passages.tafsir:
These four short ayat are the doorway to Sūrah Ar-Raḥmān, and they contain its whole argument in miniature: the Most Merciful is announced by name, and then His mercy is shown in His gifts — the Qur'an, the creation of man, and the power of speech. The sūrah as a whole, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes, continuously recounts Allah's bounties, worldly as well as spiritual; and these opening ayat name the first and greatest of them. What holds the four ayat together is that they are a single sentence of grace: *Ar-Raḥmān* is the subject, and "taught the Qur'an… created man… taught him speech" are His acts.

## Why the sūrah opens with the name "Ar-Raḥmān"

The sūrah begins, uniquely, with a single divine name standing alone as its first ayah: **Ar-Raḥmān**, the All-Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān offers two reasons for this striking choice.

First, the idolaters of Makkah were unaware of this name of Allah. They used to say, "What is Ar-Raḥmān?" — a protest the Qur'an itself records in 25:60. Opening the sūrah with this very name was a way of letting them know it.

Second, the name prepares us for the verb that follows. "Ar-Raḥmān — He taught the Qur'an." By attributing the teaching of the Qur'an to *the Most Merciful* specifically, the ayah signals that revelation is a sheer gift flowing from Allah's beneficence. Nothing obliged Him to send it; He is not in need of anyone, and no act is obligatory on Him for which He could be held responsible. The Qur'an came down as pure, unearned mercy.

The sources also tell us where this sūrah was first proclaimed. Imam Qurtubi (cited in Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān) concluded from several narratives that it was revealed in Makkah, and preferred this view. Among them is the report recorded by At-Tirmidhi from Jabir: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this sūrah to the jinn on "the night of the Jinn" — the night he met them to convey the Message of the Qur'an to them and impart knowledge to them — and that meeting took place in Makkah. So the name Ar-Raḥmān rang out first in the very city whose people asked, "What is Ar-Raḥmān?"

## The greatest bounty is named first

Notice the order of ayat 2 and 3: "He taught the Qur'an" comes *before* "He created man." In the natural order of things this is reversed — a person must exist before he can be taught, and man's creation is itself, as Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān says, a great boon and "first and foremost" in sequence. So why does the teaching of the Qur'an come first?

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān answers: because the fundamental purpose of man's creation is that he receive the knowledge of the Qur'an and live by its guidance. The commentary cites Allah's words, "And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me" (51:56) — and worship is impossible without divine guidance, whose source is the Qur'an. The order of the ayat is therefore the order of *importance*, not of time: the Book is mentioned before the being, because the being was made *for* the Book. Of all the bounties the sūrah will recount, the greatest is the knowledge of the Qur'an, an all-comprehensive Book directing man in temporal and spiritual matters, in the affairs of this world and the next. Those who heeded it and fulfilled its right, like the blessed Companions, were raised by Allah in status in the Hereafter and blessed with inconceivable bounties — and in this world too they were promoted to stations the greatest of kings were not able to attain.

## "He taught the Qur'an" — taught it to whom?

A fine point of Arabic grammar carries real meaning here. The verb *ʿallama* ("he taught") normally takes two objects: the thing taught and the person taught. In ayah 2, the first object — the Qur'an — is stated, but the second is left out. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes two ways the exegetes read this. Some said the unnamed student is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who was taught the Qur'an directly by Allah, and through him the entire creation received it. Others observed that the very omission is deliberate: because the Qur'an's purpose is to guide *all* of Allah's creation, no particular recipient is specified — the silence makes the teaching universal, embracing the totality of human beings.

Ibn Kathir adds a tender dimension to this "teaching": Allah did not merely reveal the Qur'an to His servants, He *made it easy* — easy to memorise and easy to understand for those on whom He bestows His mercy, and easy even at the physical level, teaching His servants how to recite it by making it easy for them to speak and pronounce its letters with the various parts of the mouth — the alveolar bridge, the tongue, and the lips.

## "He taught him al-bayān" — the gift of expression

Ayah 4 names one more bounty, chosen with great care: *al-bayān*, the capacity for clear expression. Al-Hasan explained it as "eloquent speech." Ibn Kathir connects it back to the Qur'an itself: this teaching of speech is bound up with Allah's teaching of the Qur'an — He enabled His servants to articulate its letters precisely so that they could recite His Book.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān widens the lens. Having created man, Allah bestowed uncountable bounties upon him — food and water, protection against cold and heat, dwelling arrangements — but these are bounties in which all creatures are equal partners. *Bayān* is singled out because it is peculiar to human beings. And it is placed immediately after the teaching of the Qur'an because the two depend on each other: deriving benefit from the Qur'an, and imparting it to others, is only possible through the knowledge of expression. The word *bayān* itself is broad — it comprehends *all* the means of communication Allah has created, like speech and writing. The various languages and dialects of the various nations of the world are all constituent parts of this linguistic knowledge, which the commentary describes as the practical interpretation and application of Allah's words, "And He taught Adam the names, all of them" (2:31).

Taken together, these four ayat ask something concrete of the reader: to recognise that your very existence, the speech on your tongue, and above all the Qur'an in your hands are gifts of Ar-Raḥmān — given freely, from sheer beneficence, and deserving of thanks.

passages.title: Cosmic order, the balance, and earth's provision
passages.tafsir:
This passage is Sūrat al-Raḥmān's opening tour of the created order: the sun and moon running on exact calculation, plants and trees bowed in submission, the sky raised and the earth laid out, and — set deliberately between the two — the balance of justice that mankind is commanded to keep. What holds ayat 5–13 together is a single idea: everything Allah made runs on measure, and the one creature given free choice is asked to bring his own dealings into the same harmony. The passage closes with the sūrah's refrain: "Then which of the blessings of your Lord will you both deny?" (ayah 13).

## A universe that keeps perfect time (ayat 5–6)

In ayah 5, "the sun and the moon travel with precision" — bi-ḥusbān. Ibn Kathir explains that they move in their orbits in perfect succession, "according to precise calculation that is never delayed nor disturbed," and he connects this to Allah's words elsewhere: "It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day. They all float, each in an orbit" (36:40), and "He has appointed the night for resting, and the sun and the moon for calculating. Such is the measuring of the Almighty, the All-Knowing" (6:96).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the key word. Some lexicologists take *ḥusbān* as an infinitive meaning "to calculate" — on the pattern of *ghufrān* (to forgive) and *qurʼān* (to recite) — so the verse means that the two bodies on which human life depends run on fixed courses, punctually performing their allotted tasks: the alternation of night and day, the change of seasons, the determination of months and years. Others take *ḥusbān* as the plural of *ḥisāb*, "calculation," in which case each of the sun and the moon has its own calculated orbits — the whole solar system proceeding on multiple simultaneous calculations, each so exact that no deviation has ever occurred. Maʿārif adds a reflection for our scientific age: every human machine, however sophisticated, breaks down and needs servicing and repair; the vast Divine creation has never once needed overhaul. That difference between human invention and Divine creation is something "every discerning person can observe."

In ayah 6, "the najm and the trees prostrate." Here the early authorities genuinely differed over *najm*, and Ibn Kathir lays out both views. Ibn ʿAbbas — as reported by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah — said it means "the plants that lay on the ground," i.e. stemless vegetation; Saʿid bin Jubayr, al-Suddi and Sufyan al-Thawri said the same, and Ibn Jarir preferred this reading — noting that whatever their disagreement over *najm*, the scholars agreed that the trees mentioned here are those "that stand on trunks." Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah, however, said *najm* means the star in the sky, and Ibn Kathir himself inclines to this as "the most obvious" meaning, citing "the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and the mountains, and the trees… prostrate themselves to Allah" (22:18). Both readings serve the passage: whether star or shrub, all of it bows.

What is this prostration? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *sajdah* is the supreme symbol of humility, surrender and obedience, and that the verse refers to what the scholars call *iṭāʿah takwīniyyah* — "compelled obedience," the obedience of things that have no choice. Allah has assigned every tree, plant and creeper a specific task for the benefit of mankind, and they perform it without the slightest deviation. There are two kinds of obedience: that of free will, given to men and jinn, who may obey or rebel; and that of the rest of creation, which simply submits. Read together, ayat 5–6 show that everything from the largest celestial body to the smallest plant is subject to Allah's laws — and Maʿārif draws the conclusion: it is inconceivable that man, for whose service this vast, perfectly regulated universe was brought into being, was himself created without purpose.

## The balance between sky and earth (ayat 7–9)

Ayah 7 says: "As for the sky, He raised it high, and set the balance." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices something subtle in the wording. The verbs *rafaʿa* ("to raise up") and *waḍaʿa* ("to put down") are antonyms — yet "placing the scale" is not the natural opposite of "raising the sky." The true opposite arrives three verses later: "And the earth He has *placed* for the creatures" (ayah 10, using the same verb *waḍaʿa*). So the Qurʼan is really describing the sky and the earth as a pair of opposites — one raised, one laid down — and has deliberately inserted a third element, the balance, between them. The wisdom, Maʿārif suggests, is that the verses which follow stress justice and fairness: the arrangement implies that the very purpose of creating the heaven and the earth was to establish justice, and that without justice there can be no peace, security or harmony on earth — only chaos, disorder and corruption. "Allah, the Pure and the Most High, knows best."

What is the *mīzān* itself? The scholars interpreted it two ways, and both are given in the sources. Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi and others took it to mean *justice* — since justice is what a scale exists for — and this is the meaning Ibn Kathir foregrounds, citing: "Indeed, We have sent Our Messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Book and the balance that mankind may keep up equity" (57:25). Other scholars took it in its plain sense: the actual weighing instrument, whether a pair of scales or any modern equivalent. Maʿārif notes that on either reading the ultimate sense is the same — maintaining rights and establishing fair dealing.

Ayah 8 gives the reason the balance was set: "so that you do not transgress in the balance." The verb *taṭghaw* comes from *ṭughyān*, which stands for injustice; verses 7 and 8 together mean the scale was created so that you would not overstep it and so practise injustice. Ibn Kathir puts it at the level of the cosmos itself: Allah "created the heavens and earth in justice and truth so that everything is founded on, and observing, justice and truth."

Ayah 9 then turns the cosmic principle into a direct command, stated twice — once positively, once negatively: "Weigh with justice (*qisṭ*, which literally means justice), and do not make the weighing deficient." The word *khusr* means to skimp, to give short measure. Maʿārif observes that the two halves are the positive and negative faces of one injunction, and Ibn Kathir sums it up plainly: do not cheat in weights and measures, but observe justice and fairness — as Allah says elsewhere, "And weigh with the true and straight balance" (26:182).

## The earth spread as a table (ayat 10–12)

Ayah 10: "He laid out the earth for all beings (*al-anām*)." Ibn Kathir's picture completes the pairing begun in ayah 7: Allah raised the heavens and laid down the earth, balancing it with firm mountains so it would be stable for its residents — creatures of every species, shape, colour and language. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd all said *al-anām* means the creatures. Maʿārif adds that al-Baydawi rendered it "everything having a soul," and notes that in this sūrah the word evidently points above all to mankind and the jinn — the two species who bear the obligations of the Sharīʿah and who are addressed throughout Sūrat al-Raḥmān in the dual form.

Ayat 11–12 then set the table. "In it are fruit" — *fākihah*, which Maʿārif defines as the fruits eaten after a meal for pleasure, of "various colors, taste and scent" in Ibn Kathir's phrase — "and palm trees with sheaths (*akmām*)." Ibn Kathir says the date palm is singled out because of its benefit both fresh and dried, and reports from Ibn Jurayj that Ibn ʿAbbas explained *akmām* as the sheathed fruit stalks in which the dates form — the cluster beginning as unripe green dates and ripening stage by stage. Maʿārif adds the lexical detail: *akmām* is the plural of *kimm*, the protective cover that surrounds dates and other fruit at the start of their growth.

Then "grain with husks, and aromatic plants" (ayah 12). *Ḥabb* is grain — wheat, rice, lentils and the like. On *ʿaṣf* the reports from Ibn ʿAbbas converge: ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported from him that it means straw, while al-ʿAwfi reported from him that it is the green leaves cut from the stem, called *ʿaṣf* once dried — and Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Abu Malik likewise said straw. Maʿārif dwells on why the husk deserves mention at all: every grain a person eats several times a day was fashioned by Allah from soil and water in wonderful ways, protected inside its cover against insects until maturity — and the husk itself is not waste but fodder for the animals whose milk nourishes us and who carry us and our loads. Even the chaff is a bounty.

*Rayḥān* carries more than one reported meaning. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said it means leaves — green leaves in the report of ʿAli bin Abi Talhah — while al-Hasan said sweet-scented plants, and Ibn Zayd likewise took it as fragrant flowers. Ibn Kathir judges that the verse describes crops that yield straw, such as wheat and barley, with *rayḥān* as the leaves on their stems — "and Allah knows best." Maʿārif adds a further shade: *rayḥān* is sometimes used for livelihood itself, as in the Arabic saying rendered "I came out looking for sustenance provided by Allah" — and Ibn ʿAbbas interpreted the word in this vein too. Fragrance, foliage, sustenance: the reports gather up all three.

## The refrain and its answer (ayah 13)

"Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?" The dual address — *rabbikumā*, "the Lord of you two" — is directed, as Mujahid and others said, to mankind and the jinn, the two species addressed throughout the sūrah. The word *ālāʼ* means favours, boons, blessings. Ibn Kathir explains the force of the question: these favours surround you on every side — you cannot honestly deny them.

The sources preserve a moving moment connected to this refrain. Al-Tirmidhi recorded from Jabir that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited Sūrat al-Raḥmān to his Companions from beginning to end, and they said nothing. He ﷺ said: "I recited it to the jinn on the night of the jinn, and their response was better than yours. Whenever I came to His statement, 'Then which of the blessings of your Lord will you both deny?' they said: 'None of Your favours do we deny, our Lord — to You belongs all praise.'" Al-Tirmidhi remarked, "This hadith is gharīb" — a technical term of hadith grading which literally means "rare" or "unusual," used for a report that reaches the collector through limited channels of transmission — and al-Bazzar also collected it. Ibn Jarir recorded a similar report from ʿAbdullah bin ʿUmar, in which the Prophet ﷺ asked, "Why do I hear the jinn giving a better response to their Lord than you?" — al-Bazzar collected this one as well.

Ibn Kathir draws the practical lesson directly: "So we say, just as the believers among the jinn said, 'O Allah! None of Your favours do we deny. All praise is due to You.'" Ibn ʿAbbas himself used to answer the refrain, saying: "Nay, our Lord!" — meaning, none of Your favours do we deny. The refrain, in other words, is not left hanging: the sources themselves model the answer — acknowledgment and praise — and, in Ibn Kathir's words, invite us to say it too.

passages.title: Humans from clay, jinn from fire
passages.tafsir:
This short passage is Sūrat al-Raḥmān's answer to a basic human question: where did we come from, and where did the unseen beings who share this world with us come from? In two tightly parallel statements, Allah names the origin of mankind (ayah 14) and the origin of the jinn (ayah 15), then turns to both together with the sūrah's famous refrain: "Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?" (ayah 16). What binds the three ayat into a unit is that very pairing — man and jinn, clay and fire — the two kinds of creation being addressed side by side and reminded of their Lord.

## Ayah 14 — man from ringing clay

"He created humankind from ˹sounding˺ clay like pottery."

The Arabic repays a close look, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up each word:

- **Al-insān ("man")** here refers — unanimously, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes — to Ādam (peace be upon him). The ayah is describing the original creation of man.
- **Ṣalṣāl ("sounding clay")** is wet soil once it has become dry and heavy — clay so dried out that, as the translation's word "sounding" suggests, it rings.
- **Fakhkhār ("pottery")** is wet soil once it has been baked. So the ayah compares Ādam's clay, dried to hardness, to the fired clay of the potter.

Ibn Kathir summarises the meaning simply: Allah created mankind from clay "like that used in pottery". The humble material is the point: man's beginning was dried mud, the stuff of a potter's workshop.

## Ayah 15 — the jinn from a smokeless flame

"And created jinn from a ˹smokeless˺ flame of fire."

Again the key words carry the meaning:

- **Al-jānn**: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records both understandings found in the sources — that jānn refers to the class of beings called jinn, and (in its rendering of the ayah) that it names the father of the jinn. Either way, the ayah is telling us the origin of that species.
- **Mārij**: the smokeless flame of fire. Ibn Kathir relates from Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn ʿAbbās — a view shared by ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd — that the jinn were created "from the tip of the flame". In another report, Al-ʿAwfī transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās: "From the best part of the fire, from its smokeless flame." Not the smoky, sooty part of a fire, but its pure, clean flame.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a precise qualification worth keeping: the smokeless flame is the *major element* in the creation of the jinn, just as dry sounding clay is the *major element* in the creation of man. The ayat name the dominant substance of each species' origin.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here the hadith that completes the picture. Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿĀʼishah that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: "The angels were created from light, the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire, and Ādam from what was described to you." Muslim also collected this hadith. It sets the three orders of creation side by side — angels of light, jinn of smokeless flame, man of clay — and its closing phrase, "from what was described to you," points to the clay of the Qurʼān's own account, exactly what ayah 14 describes.

## Ayah 16 — the refrain, addressed to both

"Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?"

The address is in the dual — "you *both*" — and after these two ayat we see why: the sūrah is speaking to the two species just named, mankind and the jinn together. Each has just been told its own origin at the hand of the same Lord — one fashioned from clay, the other from flame — and each is now confronted with the question. Ibn Kathir notes that this refrain, which recurs through the sūrah, was explained earlier in his tafsir; here it follows immediately upon the account of how both species were created.

## Reading the passage whole

Set side by side, the two creation statements do several things at once:

**They introduce the sūrah's two audiences by their origins.** The refrain speaks in the dual — to men and jinn — and these ayat present both by telling each where it came from, before the refrain returns again and again in the ayat that follow.

**They teach the unseen without speculation.** We are told what we need to know about the jinn — that they are real, created beings with a defined origin, made from the pure smokeless flame — on the authority of the Qurʼān and the Prophet ﷺ, with the early authorities (Ibn ʿAbbās and those who followed him) clarifying the wording. The passage gives certainty about the unseen while leaving its details with Allah.

**They humble both species.** Clay and flame are created materials; neither confers any claim over the Creator. Whatever differences exist between man and jinn, both stand in the same position before their Lord: fashioned by Him and answerable to Him — which is precisely the note ayah 16 strikes.

For the believer, the takeaway is the one the refrain itself demands: to hear "He created humankind from sounding clay" and respond not with denial or indifference but with acknowledgment of the Lord who made us.

passages.title: The two easts, two seas, and sailing ships
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a tour of Allah's favours across the widest horizons of the created world: the turning points of the sun in the sky, the meeting of fresh and salt waters on the earth, the treasures drawn up from the deep, and the great ships that ride upon it. What binds ayat 17–25 together is a single argument, pressed home four times by the refrain, "Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?" (ayat 18, 21, 23, 25): every one of these vast, orderly wonders is a *blessing* — the ayah's word is *ālāʼ*, favours — and each one testifies that its Lord is one.

## The two easts and the two wests (ayah 17)

The wording of ayah 17 is deliberately precise: not "the east and the west," but *rabbu l-mashriqayn wa rabbu l-maghribayn* — "Lord of the **two** easts and Lord of the **two** wests," using the Arabic dual form. Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explain the dual the same way: the sun does not rise from one fixed point all year. It rises at one point on the eastern horizon in summer and a different point in winter, and likewise sets at two different points in the west. Those two turning points of the year are the "two easts" and "two wests."

Ibn Kathir shows how the Qurʼān speaks of this same reality at three levels of resolution. Here it is the dual — the summer and winter extremes. In Sūrah al-Maʿārij (70:40) Allah swears "by the Lord of all the points of sunrise and sunset" in the plural, referring to the different places from which the sun rises and then sets on people every single day. And in Sūrah al-Muzzammil (73:9) it is the simple singular, "Lord of the east and the west; none has the right to be worshipped but He" — the two directions taken as a whole. Singular, dual, and plural are all true descriptions of one seamless order, and Ibn Kathir notes that this constant variation is not a mere astronomical curiosity: it brings real benefits to the created — mankind and jinn alike.

Notice too the word that carries the verse: *Rabb*, Lord. The One who owns, sustains, and manages both extremities of the sky is one Lord. Whoever tracks the sun through the year is watching a single hand at work.

## The two seas and the barrier (ayat 19–20)

Ayah 19 says *maraja l-baḥrayni yaltaqiyān* — "He has *maraja* the two seas, meeting together." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the verb *maraja* literally means "to let loose," and Ibn Kathir records the same meaning from Ibn ʿAbbās: Allah has let the two seas loose so that they meet. The "two seas" (*baḥrayn*), as both commentaries state, are the two kinds of water: the sweet, fresh water that comes from running rivers, and the salty water of the seas.

Then ayah 20 delivers the wonder: "between them is a *barzakh* they never cross." A *barzakh* is a barrier or partition. The two waters are *let loose* — and yet they do not transgress upon one another. Ibn Zayd, cited by Ibn Kathir, put it simply: "He prevents them from meeting by the dividing barrier He placed between them to separate them." Ibn Kathir explains the point of the barrier: if the waters transgressed upon each other, each would spoil the characteristics the other was created with — and it is precisely those distinct characteristics that make each water what it is.

Ibn Kathir connects this to the fuller statement in Sūrah al-Furqān (25:53): "It is He Who has let free the two seas: one palatable and sweet, and the other salty and bitter; and He has set a barrier and a complete partition between them." He understands the barrier as a barrier of land that Allah has placed between the two kinds of water. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the observable detail: places where the two seas meet are found in every region of the world, and wherever sweet and salty waters meet there is a distinct barrier between them — in some cases the two waters can be seen distinctly, one lying higher and the other lower; and if the salty water overrides the sweet, the sweet water's characteristics are not spoiled, nor are the salty water's affected when the sweet overrides it. The two descriptions are complementary, not competing: one commentary points to the land set between the waters, the other to the restraint seen where the waters themselves meet. Either way, restraint is built into creation by its Lord.

## Pearls and coral (ayah 22)

"Out of both come forth *al-luʼluʼ* and *al-marjān*." *Luʼluʼ* is the well-known word for pearl. On *marjān* the early authorities differed, and Ibn Kathir records both views: Mujāhid, Qatādah, Abū Ruzayn, and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said it means small pearls — a view also reported from ʿAlī — while others among the Salaf, as mentioned by Ibn Jarīr, said it means large, precious pearls. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes it as one of the precious jewels or gems: a hard substance formed from coral, which has branches like trees. All agree on the essential point — these are jewels that Allah brings out of the waters as adornment for the people of the earth.

Ibn Kathir also transmits a striking report recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim from Ibn ʿAbbās — a report whose chain of narrators, he notes, is Ṣaḥīḥ (authentic): "When it rains, the oysters in the sea open their mouths. What falls in them, the drops, turns into pearls." The image joins sky and sea in a single act of provision — rain from above becoming jewels below.

One question the wording raises: the ayah says pearls and coral come out of *both* waters, yet they are generally understood to be fished from the salt waters, not the fresh. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a reconciliation: these gems *originate* in the sweet waters, where it is not easy to hunt for them or fish them out; the sweet waters then flow into the salty seas, carrying and depositing their substances, and it is from there that the pearls and corals are brought out. Hence they truly come from both, though the salty sea is named as their source because that is where they are harvested. And Ibn Kathir draws the lesson the refrain then presses: since this kind of adornment is a favour from Allah to the people of the earth, He reminds them of it.

## The ships like mountains (ayah 24)

"And His are *al-jawāri l-munshaʼāt* in the sea, like *aʿlām*." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the words. *Jawārī* is the plural of *jāriyah*, one of whose meanings is a ship — and that is the sense in which it is used in this verse. *Munshaʼāt* comes from the root *nashaʼa*, "to rise up high, to be lofty," and so refers to the ships' lofty sails. Ibn Kathir records Mujāhid's crisp definition: "Whatever ship hoists a sail, it is from the *munshaʼāt*; if it does not hoist a sail, it is not from the *munshaʼāt*." He also notes other readings among the early scholars: Qatādah said *munshaʼāt* means "created," and others read it *munshiʼāt*, "launched." *Aʿlām* means mountains: the great ships, sails raised high, sit on the sea like mountains in their size.

The subtle theology is in the opening words: *wa lahu* — "and **His** are" the ships. Human beings build ships, yet the Qurʼān assigns them to Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the verse describes the wisdom of the making of the ship and of its running on the surface of the water — the whole enterprise, from construction to voyage, unfolds within Allah's design. And Ibn Kathir spells out the favour concretely: these mountain-like vessels make trade and commerce possible, transporting cargo from one area to another and from one province to another, providing people with the various goods they need.

## The refrain: "which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?" (ayat 18, 21, 23, 25)

Four times in these nine ayat the question returns, and its grammar is dual: *rabbikumā... tukadhdhibān* — "your Lord" and "will you both deny," addressed to two parties. Ibn Kathir's commentary on this section identifies them: mankind and the jinn, the two classes of creation whose origins were described just before this passage (ayat 14–15), and to whom the variation of sunrises and sunsets brings its benefits. Both races live under the same alternating sun, drink from the same guarded waters, and profit from the same seas — so both are asked the same unanswerable question.

And the question is unanswerable by design. Each wonder in this passage is framed not as a spectacle but as a favour, a blessing. The ordered turning of sunrise and sunset is a gift; the barrier that keeps each water true to its nature is a gift; pearls and coral are a gift; the ships that float, carrying goods across the seas, are a gift. To deny any of these is to deny what is plainly before one's eyes. The believer's response is the opposite: to look at the turning sun, the meeting seas, and the sail on the horizon, and recognize in each of them the one Lord — *Rabb* of the two easts and the two wests — whose favours cannot honestly be denied.

passages.title: All perishes; the Majestic Lord remains
passages.tafsir:
## The passage at a glance

Qatadah captured the movement of this passage in a single sentence: "First, Allah mentioned His creatures and then He said that all of this will perish." Having spoken of His creatures, the sūrah now tells us that all of them, and all of us, will pass away. Only Allah remains. What binds ayat 26–30 into one unit is a single movement of thought: everything perishes (ayah 26), the Lord of Majesty and Honour endures (ayah 27), and precisely because He alone endures, every creature in the heavens and the earth turns to Him in need at every moment (ayah 29). Twice the refrain interrupts — "Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?" (ayat 28 and 30) — daring man and jinn to deny even this.

## "Everything on it will perish" — and why that is a favour

In ayah 26, "Every being on earth is bound to perish," the pronoun "it" refers to the earth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the earth was explicitly mentioned earlier in the sūrah — "And the earth is placed by Him for creatures" (ayah 10) — and adds that "the earth" is in any case one of those universally known things Arabic can refer to by a pronoun without naming it again. Maʿārif notes that jinn and mankind are singled out in this ayah because this sūrah is addressed throughout to these two species of Allah's creation. But this does not mean the heavens are exempt: the Qurʼān states the general rule elsewhere, "Everything will perish save His Face" (28:88), a verse both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif cite as the twin of this one. Ibn Kathir spells it out: all the residents of the earth will perish and die, and the residents of the heavens too, except whomever Allah wills.

The word for "perishing" here is *fānin*, from *fanāʼ*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up its two possible senses: first, that everything is *by nature* subject to decay — nothing created carries within itself any capacity for permanence or immortality; and second, that all things will *actually* pass away on the Day of Doom. Both are true, and the ayah holds both.

It may seem strange that the announcement of universal death sits inside a sūrah whose refrain is about *favours* — yet the refrain follows it in ayah 28 all the same. Ibn Kathir supplies the link: all the inhabitants of the earth will die and end up in the Hereafter, where Allah — Dhul-Jalāl wal-Ikrām — will judge them by His fair judgement; and it is after stating this that the refrain asks which of the Lord's blessings the two of you will deny. Death, on this reading, is not where the account closes: the Hereafter follows it, and the fair judgement of the Lord of Majesty and Honour.

## "And the Face of your Lord will remain"

Ayah 27 is the pivot of the passage, and the early scholars were careful about how it is recited. Ash-Shaʿbī said: when you have recited "Whatsoever is on it will perish," do not stop — continue reading, "And the Face of your Lord, Dhul-Jalāl wal-Ikrām, will remain forever." The two ayat are one truth; to recite the perishing without the remaining is to tell half of it. Qatadah made the same observation about the order: first Allah mentioned His creatures, then He said that all of this will perish — creation is named, then dismissed, so that what remains stands alone.

**The Face of your Lord.** Ibn Kathir affirms it plainly: only Allah's Honorable Face will remain, because our Lord, the Exalted, the Blessed, is the Ever-Living Who never dies — and he links it to the ayat where deeds are done "seeking His Face": "And keep yourself patiently with those who call on their Lord morning and afternoon, seeking His Face" (18:28), and the words of those who give charity, "We feed you seeking Allah's Face only" (76:9). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that according to the majority of the exegetes the word *wajh* here stands for the Being of Allah Himself: the meaning is that He — Self-Subsisting, All-Sustaining, Independent, Besought of all — alone abides when the whole material universe is made non-existent. Indeed, Maʿārif observes, even human reason demands that behind a universe where everything dies there must be a Being who remains and never dies: the One who created it all, the First and Final Cause.

Maʿārif also relays a second interpretation held by other exegetes: that "the Face (side) of your Lord" means *whatever is on Allah's side* — His Being and Attributes, and also every action and state of His creatures that is done for His sake and remains attached to Him. On this reading the ayah promises: everything that man, jinn and angels do for Allah's pleasure will remain under His care and attain permanence, never to perish. It is supported by the ayah, "What is with you shall end and what is with Allah shall last" (16:96) — wealth, power, comfort and discomfort all pass; what is done for Allah lasts. The two readings are not rivals so much as layers: He alone remains, and therefore only what is anchored in Him remains.

**"Your Lord."** Maʿārif draws attention to a tenderness easily missed: the "your" in "the Face of *your* Lord" is addressed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. At the very moment the ayah announces the passing of all things, Allah — the Lord of lords — declares His direct, special relationship with His Prophet ﷺ, honouring him by attaching Himself to him: *rabbuka*, "your Lord," just as elsewhere He honours him with *ʿabduhu*, "His servant."

## Dhul-Jalāl wal-Ikrām — Majesty that does not turn away

The Lord who remains is described as *Dhul-Jalāl wal-Ikrām* — full of majesty, full of honour. Ibn ʿAbbās glossed it: "Owner of greatness and pride." Ibn Kathir draws the practical consequence: a Lord so described is worthy of being revered, and thus never defied; and obeyed, and thus never disobeyed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the two halves of the name. *Jalāl* is Allah's Majesty — the Greatness, Grandeur and Tremendousness that overwhelms His creation and fills them with awe. *Ikrām* is His Honour and generosity: those who use His favours well and walk the path of truth will be granted still more by the Lord of Honour. And then comes the observation that turns the whole passage: despite being the Lord of Greatness and Majesty, Allah is not like worldly kings, who in their grandeur will not spare a glance for the poor and the petitioner. He grants their petitions and answers their calls — and the very next ayah, says Maʿārif, bears testimony to this.

This name is also a key for the one who prays. Maʿārif records — as transmitted by Ibn ʿĀmir and recorded in Tirmidhi, Nasaʼi and the Musnad of Ahmad — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Persist [in invoking Allah] with 'O Lord of Majesty and Honour'" (*aliẓẓū bi Yā Dhal-Jalāli wal-Ikrām*). The word *aliẓẓū*, Maʿārif explains from Mazhari, comes from *ilẓāẓ*, "to continue firmly in a course of action" — cling to this name, keep returning to it, and the supplication prefaced with it is readily granted. Ibn Kathir likewise cites the reported supplication built on these very attributes: "O You the Ever-Living Who sustains all that exists! O You Who created the heavens and the earth without precedence. O You Who Owns the glory and the honor, none has the right to be worshipped except You… do not abandon us to rely on ourselves even for an instant, nor on any of Your creation."

## "All in the heavens and the earth beseech Him — every day He is at some task"

Ayah 29 shows what the endurance of Dhul-Jalāl wal-Ikrām means for every creature right now. Ibn Kathir: in this ayah Allah affirms that He is Rich, free of all wants, while all creatures stand in need of Him in all conditions and situations, seeking His help willingly or unwillingly. Maʿārif fills in the picture: the earthly creatures ask for their needs in this world — sustenance, health, welfare, comfort — and for the Hereafter — forgiveness, mercy, Paradise. Even the celestial creatures, who do not eat or drink, need His mercy and grace, which surround them at all times. Countless creatures, countless needs, in every region and every language, every moment — and Maʿārif asks: who besides the Absolutely Powerful, the Lord of Majesty, could answer them all?

Hence the second clause: *kulla yawmin huwa fī shaʼn* — "every day He is at some task." Maʿārif notes that "day" here is not the ordinary twenty-four hours but time in general: at every moment His Attributes are finding fresh manifestation. He gives life to some and causes others to die; He elevates some and abases others; some He makes ill and others He cures; He lifts adversity, makes the grieving smile, grants the requests of suppliants, forgives sinners and makes them deserving of Paradise, gives power and takes it away. (Maʿārif also records a fine grammatical point: some exegetes attach "every day" to the beseeching — they ask Him constantly — while others, including the construction adopted by Mawlānā Thānawī, attach it to "He is at some task"; either way, the constancy is His.)

Ibn Kathir transmits the same meaning from the early generation: Al-Aʿmash reported from Mujahid, from ʿUbayd bin ʿUmayr, who said of "Every day He is engaged in some affair": "Of His affairs is that He answers the supplicant, or gives to the one requesting, or removes adversity, or cures the one seeking to be cured."

Notice what this does to the doctrine of ayah 26–27. A Lord who merely *outlasted* the universe might be remote. But the Lord who remains is, at this very instant, answering, giving, curing, relieving. His eternity is not idle; it is endlessly active mercy.

## Living the passage

Two favours are being pressed on man and jinn in the refrains of ayat 28 and 30, and both are easy to deny by simply never thinking of them. The first: that beyond this perishing world stands an Everlasting Lord — and, as Ibn Kathir says, the inhabitants of the earth will end up in the Hereafter, where He will judge them by His fair judgement; and nothing done for His sake is ever lost, "what is with Allah shall last" (16:96). The second: that this Majestic Lord, unlike any earthly king, attends personally to every beggar at His door, every day, in every affair.

The passage itself teaches us how to respond: recite ayah 26 and do not stop until ayah 27, as Ash-Shaʿbī counselled; anchor your deeds to the One who remains, seeking His Face as those in 18:28 and 76:9 did; and when you raise your hands, persist — as the Prophet ﷺ taught — with *Yā Dhal-Jalāli wal-Ikrām*, "O Lord of Majesty and Honour," knowing that the One so addressed is, at that very moment, "at some task" — and one of His tasks is answering you.

passages.title: Warning of judgment to jinn and humankind
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah 55 (al-Raḥmān), Ayat 31–36: The Warning of Judgment to Jinn and Humankind

In ayat 31–36 Allah addresses His two accountable creations, jinn and humankind, together and directly, with a warning: the reckoning is coming, there is no way out of it, and any attempt to flee will be turned back by fire. What binds these six ayat together is a single courtroom scene announced in advance — the summons (ayah 31), the impossibility of escape (ayah 33), and the force that seals every exit (ayah 35) — each declaration punctuated by the same refrain, \"Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?\" (ayat 32, 34, 36).

## \"We will attend to you\" — what this can and cannot mean of Allah

Ayah 31 opens with a striking verb: *sanafrughu lakum* — \"We will soon attend to you.\" Ibn Jurayj explained it as \"We shall judge you,\" and Ibn Kathir cites al-Bukhari's explanation: \"We shall recompense you. Surely, nothing will busy Allah from attending to anything else.\"

That last clause matters for our creed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the Arabic: the verb comes from *farāgh*, \"to become free from an occupation\" — the opposite of *shughl*, being busy. Used literally, it would imply that the speaker was previously occupied and has now become free. Neither sense applies to Allah; He is exalted above both. Nothing occupies Him from anything else, and He does not \"become free\" as creatures do. The expression is a well-known idiom — as Ibn Kathir notes, a person says \"I will attend to you\" even when he is not busy with anything at all. In Arabic this idiom conveys total, focused seriousness: *now it is your turn, and nothing else is on the table.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why this idiom is used here. In a verse preceding this one (ayah 29), it was mentioned that beings ask of Allah for their needs — sustenance, health and welfare, comfort, forgiveness, mercy and Paradise — and every moment He is in a state of manifesting His divinity and divine attributes in answering them. Ayah 31 announces that on the Day of Judgment all of that petitioning and answering will come to an end. Of all the divine manifestations, one alone will remain: the taking of account and the passing of judgment with absolute justice.

## Al-Thaqalān: the two \"weighty\" species

Who is being summoned? *Ayyuha al-thaqalān* — \"O you two weighty ones.\" The dual form of *thaqal*, a word meaning a burden or load, and by extension anything whose weight and *value* is well known. Ibn Kathir confirms from the hadith that the term means humans and jinn: \"Everyone will be able to hear it, except the Thaqalayn,\" and another narration explains this as \"except mankind and the jinn.\"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a beautiful sidelight from the Prophet's ﷺ words, \"Indeed I leave amongst you two weighty and valuable things\" — in some versions \"Allah's Book and my family,\" in others \"Allah's Book and my Sunnah\" — the same word, *thaqalayn*, used for what is precious and weighty. (Maʿārif reconciles the two wordings: *ʿitrah* covers family both lineal and spiritual, and so refers to all the noble Companions; the teachings of the Prophet ﷺ reached the Muslims through them, so both versions come to the same result.) In our ayah, then, jinn and humankind are called *al-thaqalān* because they are the two weightiest, most valuable ensouled creatures dwelling on the earth. There is a quiet dignity inside the warning: you are being summoned to account precisely because you matter.

## Ayah 33: the challenge no one can meet

Ayah 33 shifts the address from the honorific \"two weighty ones\" to the explicit \"O assembly of jinn and humans!\" — and issues a challenge: if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that jinn are named first here, presumably because breaking through the confines of heaven and earth would demand immense power, and Allah has given the jinn more power than human beings in such matters. Yet even they cannot do it. The commentary is explicit that the proposition is hypothetical: the verse's purpose is not to suggest such a crossing is possible, but to demonstrate the utter powerlessness of both species combined to achieve it.

Escape from what, exactly? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out two readings. If the \"penetrating\" refers to this world, the meaning is: no man or jinn can cross the bounds of the heavens and the earth to escape *death* — no one can dodge the angel of death by fleeing far enough. And even that is stated \"according to human thinking,\" for in reality no one is outside Allah's power even if he were to cross those bounds. If it refers to the Day of Reckoning, the verse declares the absolute impossibility of escaping the *accounting*: on that Day the heaven will crack open, the angels will line the sides of the earth, and people will be hemmed in from every side; whichever direction the terrified crowds run, the angels will lay siege to every route.

Ibn Kathir gives the same picture: you can never escape Allah's orders and decrees, \"because it encompasses you… you are surrounded by it wherever you may be.\" He describes the Gathering, when angels in seven rows in every direction will surround the creatures, and none will escape — *illā bi-sulṭān*, \"except with authority,\" meaning except by a commandment from Allah Himself. He connects this to other ayat: \"On that Day man will say: 'Where (is the refuge) to flee?' No! There is no refuge! Unto your Lord will be the place of rest that Day\" (75:10–12), and the description of the evildoers over whom \"no defender will they have from Allah\" (10:27).

**A note Maʿārif ul Qurʼān insists on:** this verse has nothing to do with space travel. Rockets and satellites operate far below the heaven, let alone beyond its confines. Using this ayah to \"prove\" the possibility of space exploration, the commentary says bluntly, misreads what the Qurʼān is actually saying. The verse is about the impossibility of fleeing Allah's judgment, not about orbital mechanics.

## Ayah 35: fire and smoke seal the exits

What happens to those who try to flee? Ayah 35: \"There will be sent against you both *shuwāẓ* of fire and *nuḥās*, and you will not be able to defend yourselves.\"

The early authorities defined these two words with care. From Ibn ʿAbbās (via ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah): *shuwāẓ* is the flame of fire — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies, flame *without smoke*. Abū Ṣāliḥ described it as \"the flame above the fire, below the smoke,\" and al-Ḍaḥḥāk as \"a flood of fire.\" As for *nuḥās*: Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Ṣāliḥ, Saʿīd bin Jubayr and Abū Sinān said it is the smoke of the fire — smoke with no flame in it — and Ibn Jarīr notes the Arabs indeed called fire-smoke *nuḥās*. Mujāhid and Qatādah read it differently: molten brass poured over their heads; al-Ḍaḥḥāk said liquid copper. So the two escapees are met with the two faces of fire — searing smokeless flame and blinding flameless smoke (or molten metal).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records two views on when this occurs. Some exegetes take it as describing Hell itself after the reckoning: the disbelievers will pass through regions of pure flame without smoke and regions of pure smoke without flame — two distinct modes of punishment. Others tie it directly to ayah 33: if jinn and mankind attempt to escape on the Day of Resurrection, the angels — including those who guard Hellfire — will bring them back by directing the flames of fire and smoke upon them. Ibn Kathir explains the ayah in this second way: if mankind and the jinn try to escape on the Day of Resurrection, the angels, including the guardians of Hellfire, will bring them back by directing smoke of fire and molten brass upon them. Either way, the function in the passage is the same: every exit is sealed by fire.

The closing phrase carries its own weight. *Fa-lā tantaṣirān* comes from *intiṣār*, helping someone defend himself against a calamity. So the words mean, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, that jinn and mankind will not be able to help *each other* against the divine punishment, try as they might. The two mightiest species on earth, combined, will have no defence and no ally.

## The refrain amid the warning

Three times in this passage — ayat 32, 34, 36 — the summons, the challenge, and the fire are each followed by the same question: \"Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?\" Even inside a warning, the One speaking is named as \"your Lord,\" and what He asks His two addressees about is His *favours*. The warning is delivered honestly, in advance, with the way of escape shown to be closed — and the question put to jinn and humankind after each disclosure is whether they will still deny.

## Living under this passage

The passage asks for one settled conviction: there is no geography of escape from Allah — not from death, and not from the reckoning. Ibn Kathir's phrase deserves memorising: His rule and judgment \"encompasses you… wherever you may be.\" A believer who absorbs that stops looking for exits and starts preparing an account, knowing that the One who will \"attend\" to us on that Day will judge, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, with absolute justice and equity.

passages.title: The sky splits and Hell claims the deniers
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah 55 (Al-Raḥmān), Ayat 37–45 — The sky splits and Hell claims the deniers

This passage is the terrifying centre of Sūrat al-Raḥmān's argument. Ibn Kathir gathers these ayat under one heading, "The Horrors of the Day of Resurrection," and that is what binds them: a single continuous scene. The sky itself gives way (ayah 37); the guilty are identified and seized without a word of interrogation (ayat 39–41); and Hell — the very thing they spent their lives calling a lie — stands before their eyes (ayat 43–44). Four times the scene is punctuated by the sūrah's refrain, *"Then which of the blessings of your Lord will you both deny?"* — addressed in the dual to the two whom ayah 39 itself names side by side: human and jinn.

## A melting, rose-coloured sky

Ayah 37 opens the scene: *"When the heaven is rent asunder, and it becomes wardah like dihān."* Ibn Kathir explains the image these Arabic words carry: the heavens will melt the way sediment and silver melt when heated, and they will be coloured the way dyes stain a thing — sometimes red, sometimes yellow, blue, or green. As-Suddi said, "It will be as rosy color and as filth oil"; Mujahid said *ka-l-dihān* means "like the colors of dyes." The one fixed, dependable thing above every head — the sky — becomes a shifting, molten stain of colour. Ibn Kathir notes that this is the same event described elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"And the heaven will be rent asunder, for that Day it will be frail and torn up"* (69:16), and *"When the heaven is split asunder, and listens to and obeys its Lord — and it must do so"* (84:1–2). For him, this image alone "demonstrates the extent of the horrors of the Mighty Day of Resurrection."

## No questions asked — and why that is not a contradiction

Ayah 39 says something startling: *"On that Day he will not be questioned about his sin, neither human nor jinn."* Yet Allah also swears, *"By your Lord, We shall certainly call all of them to account, for all that they used to do"* (15:92–93). The classical commentators took this apparent tension seriously, and the sources record three answers:

**Ibn ʿAbbās:** no one will be asked *whether* he committed the sin — the angels have already recorded everything in the ledger of deeds, and Allah has pre-eternal knowledge of it. The question that remains is *why* they did it. There is no fact-finding on that Day, only confrontation.

**Mujahid:** the angels of punishment will have no need to interrogate the criminals, because the guilty will already be marked — recognisable at a glance by the signs on their faces (the very marks ayah 41 describes) — and hurled into the Fire accordingly.

**Qatadah:** the ayah refers to a *stage* of the Day. First the guilty will be questioned about their sins and will deny them under oath; then their mouths and tongues will be sealed, and their hands and feet will bear witness against them. After that, no further questions will be asked.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Ibn Kathir notes all three explanations, adding: "They are close to each other, and thus there is no conflict." The Day has stages: there is a reckoning, and then there is a moment past all reckoning — and ayah 39 describes that moment, when the verdict is already written on the faces of the condemned. Ibn Kathir also links the ayah to *"That will be a Day when they shall not speak, and they will not be permitted to put forth any excuse"* (77:35–36).

## Known by their marks, seized by forelock and foot

Ayah 41: *"The criminals will be known by their sīmā"* — a word Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains simply means "a sign," a distinguishing mark. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatadah said they will be known by their dark faces and their blue eyes; Maʿārif adds from Hasan al-Basri that through grief their faces will turn pale. Ibn Kathir draws the contrast himself: this is the opposite of the mark of the believers — the light that will appear on the parts of the body they used to wash while performing ablution. On that Day, identity is not declared; it radiates. A lifetime of belief or denial becomes visible on the body.

*"…and they will be seized by the nawāṣī and the feet."* **Nawāṣī**, Maʿārif explains, is the plural of *nāṣiyah*, the forelock — the hair at the front of the head. To be taken by the forelock is the posture of total helplessness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives three readings of the phrase: some will be dragged by their forelocks and others by their feet; or each person will be dragged sometimes by the one and sometimes by the other; or — the most severe — the angels will bend the head down to the feet, bind forelock to foot, and throw them into the Fire, adding "Allah knows best." Ibn Kathir relates this last picture from Ibn ʿAbbās (through al-Aʿmash): the condemned man will be taken by his forehead and his feet and "broken just as a stick is broken to be thrown into an oven."

## "This is the Hell which the criminals denied"

Ayah 43 is a sentence spoken *to* the condemned, and its sting is in the word *denied*. Ibn Kathir gives its sense: this is the very Fire whose existence you used to deny — now you see it before your eyes. And it will be said to them, he adds, while they are being chastised, criticised, disgraced and belittled. The punishment is not only fire; it is the collapse of a lifetime's confident denial in a single act of seeing. The thing they mocked as a preacher's story is now the most real thing in front of them.

## Between the Fire and the boiling water

Ayah 44: *"They will go round between it and ḥamīm ān."* Ibn Kathir explains the alternation: at times they are punished with fire, and at times they are given **ḥamīm** to drink — a drink like molten copper that tears the intestines and internal organs, as in Allah's words: *"When the iron collars will be rounded over their necks, and the chains, they shall be dragged along in the ḥamīm, then they will be burned in the Fire"* (40:71–72). There is no relief in the movement; each station is only a different torment.

The word **ān** received close attention. Ibn Kathir explains it as hot — a fierce, intense heat impossible to bear. Ibn ʿAbbās said of the ḥamīm that it is water "that has reached the ultimate temperature and boiling fiercely" — and the same was said by Mujahid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ad-Dahhāk, al-Hasan, ath-Thawrī and as-Suddī. Qatadah added a chilling detail: "Its boiling started when Allah created the heavens and the earth!" Muhammad bin Kaʿb al-Qurazī described its effect: the disobedient servant will be seized by the forehead and stirred in that boiling water until his flesh melts and only the bones and the eyes in his head remain.

A second report from al-Qurazī — also the view of Ibn Zayd — says *ān* means "prepared." Ibn Kathir shows the two readings do not conflict: the root carries both senses in the Qur'an itself. In *"They will be given to drink from a spring, āniyah"* (88:5) it means severe, unbearable heat, while in *"not to wait for it to be prepared"* (33:53) it means something properly cooked and made ready. Ḥamīm ān is both: brought to its extreme and made ready for those it awaits.

## Why the refrain still says "blessings"

Four times in this passage of terror, Allah asks: *"Then which of the blessings of your Lord will you both deny?"* (ayat 38, 40, 42, 45). How can a description of Hell be counted among blessings? Ibn Kathir answers directly: punishing the disobedient criminals, like favouring the people of taqwā (mindful obedience of Allah), flows from Allah's grace, mercy, justice, compassion and kindness for His creatures — and His *warnings* against His torment, such as these very ayat, are themselves a favour, because they are given now, while there is still time, and "should encourage all creatures to abandon the Shirk and disobedience they engage in." The warning is the mercy. A Lord who did not care would not warn.

That is how this passage asks to be read: not as spectacle, but as a favour extended before the sky splits — while denial can still be exchanged for belief, and the mark being written on our faces is still ours to choose.

passages.title: Two Gardens for those who fear their Lord
passages.tafsir:
## The turn from terror to reward

With ayah 46 the sūrah pivots. The preceding verses described the punishments awaiting the deniers; now the same voice turns to the reward prepared for the righteous — and the whole passage (46–53) is one connected portrait: two Gardens promised to a specific kind of person, then described feature by feature, with the sūrah's famous refrain — *"Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?"* — sounding after every detail (ayat 47, 49, 51, 53). The structure itself is the message: each blessing is named, and then the question presses its hearers — addressed as "you both" — to deny it if they dare.

## Who earns the two Gardens: "the one who fears the standing before his Lord"

Everything in this passage is *for* someone: ayah 46 opens with *wa-liman khāfa maqāma rabbihi* — "for whoever fears the standing before his Lord." Both of our commentaries linger on this phrase, because it defines the character being rewarded.

According to most exegetes — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records — *maqām rabbihi* means the standing before Allah on the Day of Resurrection to give account of one's deeds. The "fear" here is not an occasional shudder but a settled mindfulness: such a person remembers, in public and in private, that one day he must appear in the Court of Allah — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "evidently such a person will never go near the sinful acts." The awe reshapes conduct.

Other exegetes, such as al-Qurṭubī, read the phrase as "the one who is fearful of the *Station* of his Lord" — that is, mindful of Allah's high station whereby He watches over his words and deeds, overt and covert, so that nothing he does is hidden from Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the two readings converge in practice: whether one fears the future standing before Allah or Allah's present watchfulness, the result is the same — a person kept away from sin at all times.

Ibn Kathir fills out the portrait by pairing this ayah with Sūrah al-Nāziʿāt: the one who fears the standing before his Lord *"and restrained himself from the desires"* (79:40). He does not indulge in or prefer this worldly life; he knows the Hereafter is better and more lasting, so he does what his Lord commands and keeps away from what He forbids — and for this he earns two Gardens from his Lord on the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Kathir also draws out something easy to miss: this ayah is general, applying to both humans and jinn — Allah is reminding *Ath-Thaqalayn* of this favour, as He asks, *"Then which of the blessings of your Lord will you both deny?"* This, he says, is proof that the jinn who believe and have taqwā (consciousness of Allah) will enter Paradise, for the reward is being held out to both alike.

## Why two Gardens — gold and silver

Why *two* Gardens for one believer? Ibn Kathir answers with the hadith recorded by al-Bukhari from ʿAbdullah bin Qays, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There are two gardens made of silver — their vessels and all that they contain. And there are two gardens made of gold — their vessels and all that they contain. And nothing stands between the people in the ʿAdn Garden and looking at their Lord, the Exalted and Most Honored, but the covering of pride before His Face." Ibn Kathir adds that "the Group," with the exception of Abu Dawud, collected this hadith via the narration of ʿAbdul-ʿAzīz.

Notice what the hadith holds together: gardens whose very vessels are gold and silver — and, beyond all of it, the promise that only the covering of pride before Allah's Face stands between the people of ʿAdn and *looking at their Lord*. The material delights are real, and yet the hadith quietly points past them to something greater.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets this passage beside ayah 62 later in the sūrah — *"And lesser than these two, there are two other gardens"* — and adopts what it calls the most plausible explanation of the two pairs: the first two Gardens (our passage) are reserved exclusively for the foremost believers granted special nearness to Allah, while the second two are for the general body of righteous believers of lesser spiritual attainment. It supports this with a Prophetic tradition cited in Bayān-ul-Qurʼān from Ad-Durr-ul-Manthūr: "There are two Gardens made of gold for believers who are granted special nearness to Allah; and there are two Gardens made of silver for the People of the Right" — the general body of the righteous. So the passage before us describes the *higher* pair; and, as we will see, its wording is consistently richer than the description of the second pair.

## The Gardens described: branches, springs, fruit

**Ayah 48 — *dhawātā afnān*, "possessing afnān."** Ibn Kathir explains that the trees of these Gardens have beautiful young branches bearing every type of ripened, beautiful fruit; he cites ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasānī and several others that *afnān* means spreading branches — branches that reach out to the branches of other trees. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the picture to its conclusion: trees abounding in branches means dense shade and fruit in abundance. And it adds a telling observation: no such quality is mentioned of the second pair of Gardens later in the sūrah — a silence that may imply their relative deficiency, another sign that this first pair is the superior one.

**Ayah 50 — two springs flowing.** In each of the two Gardens run two springs, flowing free — Ibn Kathir says they flow to water those trees and branches that produce all kinds of fruit. He records that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said one of these springs is called Tasnīm and the other As-Salsabīl, and that ʿAṭiyah said the water of one of them is from non-standing water — water that moves, not a stagnant pool — and the other from wine that gives delight to those who drink it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān again reads this verse against its counterpart: here the springs are *tajriyān*, "flowing" freely and ceaselessly, while the springs of the second pair of Gardens (ayah 66) are *naḍḍākhatān*, "gushing forth." Gushing is what every spring does; flowing on is an *additional* excellence of these particular springs. It cites the words of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib (may Allah be pleased with him), recorded in Ad-Durr-ul-Manthūr: the two springs that are flowing freely are better than the two other springs described as gushing forth.

**Ayah 52 — every fruit in pairs.** *Fīhimā min kulli fākihatin zawjān* — in both Gardens, of *every* fruit, two kinds. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the force of "of every fruit": the first two Gardens comprehend all kinds of fruit, whereas of the second pair, ayah 68 says simply "fruits." As for the pairs, it offers two possibilities: perhaps one kind dried and one fresh, or one of normal taste and one of some extraordinary flavour. Ibn Kathir opens the meaning wider still: every type and kind of fruit — those they knew before, but better, and those they never knew; delights no eye has ever seen, no ear has ever heard, no heart has ever imagined. He then records that Ibrāhīm bin al-Ḥakam bin Abān said that his father narrated from ʿIkrimah that Ibn ʿAbbās said: "There is not a fruit that exists in this life, sweet or bitter, but it exists in Paradise, even the colocynth" — the proverbially bitter fruit standing at the far end of the saying's "sweet or bitter." And Ibn ʿAbbās also said: "There is nothing in the world that is in the Hereafter except in name" — meaning, as Ibn Kathir explains, the difference and contrast between the two in enjoyment and value is enormous: what Paradise shares with this world is the names of things, not their measure.

## The refrain, and what the passage asks of us

Four times in eight ayat — after the Gardens are promised, after the branches, after the springs, after the fruit — comes the same question: *"Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?"* Each blessing is held up individually, and both audiences — humans and jinn, as Ibn Kathir explains — are pressed to answer. The refrain turns description into testimony: these are not decorations but *ālāʾ*, favours of the Lord, and denying any of them is what the question exposes as indefensible.

And the door into all of it is the passage's first phrase. What is rewarded here is not a feat beyond ordinary reach but a state of heart: living — in public and in private — as one who knows he will stand before Allah, and who therefore restrains his soul from its desires. The sūrah's logic is generous: the fear of that standing is precisely what these two Gardens are given *for*, so the very awe that holds a believer back from sin today is what opens the gold and silver Gardens tomorrow — and, beyond them, what the hadith holds out as the crowning promise: the people of ʿAdn looking at their Lord.

passages.title: Reclining in luxury; goodness repaid with goodness
passages.tafsir:
These ayat carry us inside the two Gardens: the rest enjoyed there, the nearness of every delight, the pure companions — and then the whole description is sealed with a single luminous principle that explains why any of it is given at all: "Is there any reward for good other than good?" (ayah 60). What holds the passage together is movement from the *scene* of bliss to its *reason*: reclining in luxury, and goodness repaid with goodness.

## Rest, and delight within arm's reach (ayah 54)

The passage opens with a posture: *muttakiʾīn* — "reclining". Ibn Kathir explains that the residents of Paradise will recline or sit cross-legged. It is the body language of complete ease: no labour, no standing to serve, no anxiety left to sit upright for.

They recline "on furnishings lined with *istabraq*". Istabraq is thick silk brocade — so say the early commentators ʿIkrimah, Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah; Abu ʿImran Al-Jawni adds that it is "thick silk embroidered with gold". Notice what the ayah chooses to describe: not the upper surface of these furnishings, but their **lining** — the part that faces the floor, the part no one is meant to see. Ibn Kathir draws out the point: the honour of the outside is alluded to by mentioning the honour of the inside. ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud put it memorably: "This is their interior, so what about it if you see their exterior?" If the hidden underside is gold-embroidered silk, the visible surface is beyond describing — a rhetorical device that leaves the imagination reaching upward.

Then: "and the fruit of the two Gardens will be near at hand" — *jana … dān*. Ibn Kathir explains that the fruit will be close to the believers, who may take whatever they wish **whether reclining or otherwise** — the fruit descends from its branches to whoever desires it. He links this to the same picture elsewhere in the Qurʼan: "The fruits in bunches whereof will be low and near at hand" (69:23), and "the bunches of fruit thereof will hang low within their reach" (76:14). In this world, comfort and effort trade off against each other; you rest *or* you reach. In Paradise the reaching is abolished. The blessing comes to the blessed.

## The companions: modest, untouched, radiant (ayat 56 and 58)

In ayah 56, "wherein" — Ibn Kathir notes this means upon those very couches — will be *qāṣirāt aṭ-ṭarf*, "maidens of modest gaze": wives who restrain their glances, desiring none but their husbands, and seeing their husbands as the most beautiful men in Paradise. This is the explanation of Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, ʿAtaʼ Al-Khurasani and Ibn Zayd. The phrase describes a love that is exclusive from the inside — not enforced, but felt. It was reported that one of these wives will say to her husband: "By Allah! I neither see anything in Paradise more handsome than you nor more beloved to me than you. So praise be to Allah Who made you for me and made me for you." Even marital delight in Paradise resolves into praise of Allah.

The ayah continues: "whom no human has touched before them, nor jinn." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the verb: *ṭamth* has more than one meaning in Arabic — it can denote menstrual discharge (a menstruating woman is called *ṭāmith*), and it can mean intercourse with a virgin; it is this second sense intended here. These companions are untouched, pure for their spouses alone.

Ibn Kathir draws a striking doctrinal point from the wording "nor jinn": the ayah is proof that **the believers among the jinn will enter Paradise**. Artat bin Al-Mundhir related that Damrah bin Habib was asked whether the jinn will enter Paradise and answered: "Yes, and they will get married. The jinn will have jinn women and the humans will have female humans."

Ayah 58 gives their description in two images: "as if they were *yāqūt* and *marjān*" — rubies and coral. Mujahid, Al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and others explained: "They are as pure as rubies and white as marjān" — and here, Ibn Kathir notes, the early scholars described *marjān* as pearls. The comparison is not to ornament but to purity itself: the purity of the ruby, the whiteness of the pearl.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir cites two hadiths under these ayat.

First, Imam Muslim recorded from Muhammad bin Sirin that people once wondered — or boasted — over whether men or women are more numerous in Paradise. Abu Hurayrah settled it by recalling the words of Abu Al-Qasim ﷺ: "Verily, the first group that will enter Paradise will look like the moon when it is full, and the next batch will be as radiant as the radiant star in the sky. Each one of them will marry two wives. The marrow of the bones of their shins will be seen through the flesh. None will be unmarried in Paradise." Ibn Kathir notes this hadith was recorded in the Two Sahihs. Its imagery sits naturally beside the ayah's: bodies radiant as the moon and stars, so purified that even the marrow shines through the flesh — an echo of the exegetes' words, "as pure as rubies."

Second, Imam Ahmad recorded that Anas said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A morning or an evening journey in Allah's cause is better than the world and whatever is on its surface. And a place in Paradise as small as that occupied by the whip of one of you is better than the world and whatever is on its surface. If one of the women of the people of Paradise looks directly at the earth, she will fill what is between Paradise and earth with a good scent, and all of it will become delightful. Verily, the veil over her head is better than this life and all that is on its surface." Al-Bukhari also collected a similar narration. The hadith performs a kind of exchange-rate calculation: a whip's-length of Paradise outweighs the entire world — which is exactly why a single morning's striving for Allah is the better bargain.

## The principle beneath it all (ayah 60)

Then comes one of the most quoted lines in the Qurʼan: *hal jazāʼu al-iḥsāni illā al-iḥsān* — "Is there any reward for good other than good?" The same Arabic word, *iḥsān* (goodness, the doing of good), appears on both sides of the sentence: iḥsān from the servant is answered with iḥsān from the Lord.

Ibn Kathir explains: Allah declares that in the Hereafter, good and righteousness is the only befitting reward for those who did good in this life — as He says elsewhere, "For those who have done good is the best reward, and even more" (10:26). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it as a settled principle: having described the two Gardens for the intimate believers, it is declared that a good deed attracts a good reward — the righteous believers will therefore be blessed with good rewards.

But Ibn Kathir adds a caution that keeps the theology straight: all of these tremendous blessings **cannot be earned merely by good deeds** — they come by Allah's favour and bounty. The rhetorical question of ayah 60 is not a wage contract, as if silk-lined couches were the market price of our prayers; it is a promise of Allah's generosity. He meets goodness with goodness — and then gives beyond it, from pure grace.

## The refrain that will not let go (ayat 55, 57, 59, 61)

Four times in eight ayat the question returns: "Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?" It falls after the couches and the near-at-hand fruit, after the modest-eyed companions, after the rubies and coral, and — most pointedly — immediately after the principle of ayah 60. As if to say: even the *rule* that goodness is repaid with goodness is itself a favour that could never justly be denied. The refrain turns a description of Paradise into a standing interrogation of the reader: all this is offered — what exactly would you call a lie?

passages.title: Two further Gardens of deep green
passages.tafsir:
This passage opens the second of the two great Paradise scenes of Sūrah ar-Raḥmān. Having described two Gardens earlier in the sūrah — the Gardens Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls "the two Gardens for the intimate believers" — Allah now announces **two further Gardens**: "and below these two, two other Gardens" (ayah 62), and describes them in the same rhythm: their deep green colour, their springs, their fruits, each gift sealed with the refrain, "Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?" What holds the ayat together is a single, deliberate act of comparison: every description here answers a description given earlier, and the differences are the message.

## Two more Gardens — and who they are for

The little phrase *min dūnihimā* in ayah 62 — "below these two" — carries the weight of the whole passage. Ibn Kathir explains that these two Gardens are lower **in virtue and in status** than the two mentioned before them. He recalls the hadith mentioned earlier in the sūrah's tafsir: there are two gardens made of gold, their vessels and all they contain, and two gardens made of silver, their vessels and all they contain. The first two are for the near believers — the *Muqarribin* — and the latter two are for those on the right, *Ashab Al-Yamin*. Abu Musa commented: "There are two gardens made of gold for the Muqarribin and two gardens made of silver for Ashab Al-Yamin."

So Paradise, in this sūrah, is tiered. The passage before this one described the reward of one rank; this passage describes the reward of the rank behind them — still believers, still honoured beyond imagination, but a degree lower.

## Reading the two passages side by side

Ibn Kathir draws out several proofs that the first two Gardens outrank these two, and his method is worth following closely, because it teaches how precisely the Qur'an chooses its words:

**The order itself.** Allah mentioned the first two Gardens before these, "thus indicating their significance" — and then said *min dūnihimā*, "below these two", which Ibn Kathir calls "an obvious form of honoring the first two gardens over the latter two."

**Branches versus colour.** The first Gardens were described as *dhawātā afnān* — "with Afnān", the extending branches, or various types of delights. These are described in ayah 64 with a single word: *mudhāmmatān*, dark. Ibn Kathir comments that the first Gardens' branches are "fresh, youthful and intermingling", and there is no doubt they are the better of the two pairs.

**Flowing versus gushing.** In the first Gardens, "two springs flowing free"; here, in ayah 66, two springs *naddakhatan* — gushing. ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reports from Ibn ʿAbbas: "It means gushing. And the free flowing is stronger than gushing." Ad-Dahhak adds that it means the springs are full of water and constantly gushing. A gushing spring is a marvel — but a spring that runs freely and continuously is greater still.

**Every fruit versus named fruits.** The first Gardens contained "every kind of fruit in pairs"; these, in ayah 68, contain "fruits, and date palms and pomegranates." Ibn Kathir: there is no doubt that the first description is better and "refers to more of a variety and more types of fruit." The earlier, open-ended phrase promised something beyond any list.

## Mudhāmmatān — a whole verse in one word

Ayah 64 is a single Arabic word, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over it. *Mudhāmmatān* means "both dark green with foliage."
