It derives from *idhimām*, which describes a meadow or garden that has become so deeply green that its green inclines toward black — and it becomes that way "by reason of abundance of moisture or irrigation." Ibn ʿAbbas said the two Gardens "have become dark green because of extensive water irrigation," and Muhammad bin Kaʿb said simply: "full of greenery."

Anyone who has seen well-watered land understands the image. Green so dense it looks almost black is the colour of land saturated with water and bursting with life. In one word, the ayah conveys lushness, abundance, and endless irrigation.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds an important caution about how to read these comparisons: the fact that "dark green" is said of these Gardens and not of the first two does **not** mean the first two lack that quality. The first Gardens were described as having a lot of branches, "and this comprehends the quality of 'dark green' as well." In other words, the descriptions of the lesser Gardens are true of the greater ones too; the greater ones simply have more. The comparison never diminishes these two Gardens — it elevates the others above an already overwhelming standard.

## The refrain — ayat 63, 65, 67, 69

Four of these eight ayat are the sūrah's signature question: "Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?" It falls after every single gift — after the announcement of the Gardens, after their colour, after their springs, after their fruit — so that no blessing passes without the two addressees being asked to acknowledge it. Even the "lesser" tier of Paradise is pressed upon the hearer, favour by favour, as something no honest heart could deny.

## What this asks of the believer

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames the whole Paradise section of this sūrah with the principle declared in ayah 60: "Is there any reward for goodness other than goodness?" A good deed attracts a good reward; the righteous believers will be blessed with good rewards. That is the engine behind both pairs of Gardens.

And the tiering itself is instruction. These ayat tell the believer two things at once: first, that even the lower rank of Paradise is a place of gardens dark with foliage, gushing springs, date palms and pomegranates — no one who reaches it has lost anything; and second, that above it stand the two Gardens of the Muqarribin, the near believers. The passage comforts and beckons in the same breath.

passages.title: Pure companions and cushioned repose in the Gardens
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

Ayat 70–77 complete the Qurʼān's portrait of the second pair of Gardens in Sūrat al-Raḥmān — the two Gardens introduced at ayah 62 with the words "and below these two, there are two other Gardens." Having described their deep greenery, their gushing springs and their fruit, the sūrah now turns to what awaits the believer *inside*: companions of good character and beautiful form (ayat 70, 72, 74) and furnishings of luxurious repose (ayah 76). Each blessing is punctuated by the sūrah's recurring refrain — "Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?" (ayat 71, 73, 75, 77) — so that no favour is allowed to pass unacknowledged.

## Two pairs of Gardens — and why the wording differs

To read these ayat well, you need the frame Ibn Kathir builds around them. These two Gardens, he says, are lower in virtue and in status than the two mentioned before them, and the Qurʼān itself supports this. He recalls the hadith he cited earlier in this sūrah's tafsir: there are two gardens made of gold, their vessels and all they contain, and two gardens made of silver, their vessels and all they contain — the first two for the near believers (the *Muqarrabīn*), the latter two for those on the right (*Aṣḥāb al-Yamīn*). Abu Musa commented: "There are two gardens made of gold for the Muqarribin and two gardens made of silver for Ashab Al-Yamin."

Ibn Kathir then does something valuable for the careful reader: he shows that the Qurʼān's own word choices grade the two pairs. Allah mentioned the first pair before the second — itself a form of honouring them — and then described them differently. The first Gardens have *afnān*, extending branches (or, on another explanation, various types of delights); the second are simply *mudhāmmatān* — so intensely irrigated they have turned dark. Ibn 'Abbas explained: "they have become dark green because of extensive water irrigation," and Muhammad bin Ka'b said it means "full of greenery." The first have "two springs flowing free"; the second have springs that are *naḍḍākhatān*, gushing — and 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the free flowing is stronger than the gushing. The first contain "every kind of fruit in pairs"; the second "fruits, and date palms and pomegranates" — real abundance, but, as Ibn Kathir notes, the first description refers to more variety and more types of fruit. Every description of the second pair is glorious in itself, yet each sits a degree beneath its counterpart. That same graded comparison continues in our passage, in the description of the companions. The lesson underneath it is one of Paradise's ranks: even the "lesser" Gardens are Gardens of silver whose delights defy imagination — and beyond them lies more.

## Ayah 70 — "good and gorgeous": beauty of character before beauty of form

*Fīhinna khayrātun ḥisān* — "In them are *khayrāt ḥisān*." Two readings of *khayrāt* are transmitted. Qatadah took it broadly: there are various types of good and delightful things in these two Gardens. But the majority of scholars, Ibn Kathir reports, read *khayrāt* as the plural of *khayrah*: a righteous, well-mannered, beautiful woman — and he notes this explanation is also reported from Umm Salamah as a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the precision of the two adjectives, and it is worth pausing on. *Khayrāt* (translated "good") refers to "the good character of those women"; *ḥisān* (translated "gorgeous") refers to "women who have beautiful features." So in a single two-word phrase the Qurʼān names inner virtue first and outward beauty second — goodness of soul, then loveliness of form. Ibn Kathir records another hadith in which al-Ḥūr al-ʿAyn — the maidens of Paradise — will sing: "We are Al-Khayrat Al-Hisan, we were created for honorable husbands." Their very song joins the two qualities together — and adds a third point: they are created *for* the honoured believers. The companionship of Paradise is not incidental; it is prepared and bestowed. Maʿārif adds that these qualities are common to the maidens of both pairs of Gardens — the difference between the ranks lies elsewhere.

## Ayah 72 — reserved in pavilions

*Ḥūrun maqṣūrātun fī al-khiyām* — "maidens with gorgeous eyes, reserved in pavilions." Here Ibn Kathir's comparative method illuminates again. Of the first Gardens Allah said *fīhinna qāṣirāt al-ṭarf* (55:56) — companions "restraining their glances." Of these Gardens He says they are "guarded in pavilions." Ibn Kathir writes that there is no doubt that the chaste wives who restrain their glances themselves are better than those guarded in pavilions — even though both are secluded. Once again the two descriptions are each noble, and one sits a degree above the other. This is the kind of detail that rewards reading the Qurʼān slowly.

**The pavilion itself is no small thing.** Al-Bukhari recorded that 'Abdullah bin Qays narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Verily, in Paradise, the believer will have a tent from a hollow pearl, the width thereof is sixty miles. In each corner of it there are wives for the believer that do not see the other wives, and the believer will visit them all." In another narration the Prophet ﷺ said that this tent is thirty miles wide. Muslim also recorded this hadith, and in his narration the Prophet ﷺ said: "Verily in Paradise, the believer will have a tent made of a hollow pearl the length thereof being sixty miles. In it, the believer will have wives who do not see each other, and the believer will visit them all." Let the image settle: the *khiyām* — "tents" — of ayah 72 are not tents as this world knows them, but single hollowed pearls of staggering scale. When the Qurʼān speaks of Paradise in the vocabulary of this world, the words are familiar; the realities behind them are not.

## Ayah 74 — untouched purity

"No human or jinn has ever touched these maidens before." Ibn Kathir observes that this meaning was already explained earlier in the sūrah, and he does not repeat it here. He then points out the grading once more, this time in what is *added* elsewhere: of the first Gardens' companions Allah went on to say, "they are like Yaqut (rubies) and Marjan (pearls)" (55:58) — an extra ornament of description that the second pair's companions do not receive.

## Ayah 76 — green cushions and splendid carpets

*Muttakiʼīna ʿalā rafrafin khuḍrin wa-ʿabqariyyin ḥisān* — "reclining on green *rafraf* and beautiful *ʿabqarī*." The posture itself speaks: *muttakiʼīn*, reclining — the position of one at ease and at rest.

What is *rafraf*? 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reports from Ibn 'Abbas: cushions — and Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, Qatadah, ad-Dahhak and others said the same. Al-'Ala' bin Badr adds a visual detail: the *rafraf* are "arrayed hanging over the couches" — draped luxuriance, not mere seating. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān brings the lexicons to bear: the Qāmūs explains *rafraf* as a silk fabric, greenish in colour, used in making carpets, pillows, cushions and other items of decoration, and the Arabic lexicon Ṣiḥāḥ adds that these are embellished with arboreal and floral patterns — what Urdu calls *mushajjar*. So the green of these Gardens is not only in their deep-watered foliage (*mudhāmmatān*, ayah 64); it is woven into the very cloth the believers rest upon.

And *ʿabqarī*? Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, ad-Dahhak and as-Suddi explained it as rich carpets; Maʿārif, again citing the lexicon, gives its broader sense — "every fine, beautiful fabric or material" — with *ḥisān*, "beautiful," qualifying it.

## The refrain, four times

Four times in these eight ayat — after the companions of good character, after the pavilions, after their purity, after the cushioned rest — comes the question: *fa-bi-ayyi ālāʼi rabbikumā tukadhdhibān*, "Then which of your Lord's favours will you both deny?" Each blessing is held up individually, and after each one the question returns, in effect: *this one — will you deny this one?* No favour is allowed to blur into the next; each demands its own acknowledgment. The passage then leads directly into the verse with which the sūrah closes — "Blessed be the Name of your Lord, Dhil-Jalāli wal-Ikrām" (55:78).

## Living it

Two things follow from this passage for the believer. First, hope with striving: even the second rank of Paradise — the silver Gardens of those on the right — contains pearl pavilions of staggering scale, companions of good character and beautiful form, and rest upon green patterned silk. No one who reaches any Garden has lost. Yet the Qurʼān's own graded wording, as Ibn Kathir traced it, is a summons upward: there is a nearer rank, and it is worth striving for. Second, the refrain's discipline of gratitude: to hear blessing after blessing named and answer, each time, *none of Your favours do we deny* — and to live in this world the way that answer requires.

passages.title: Blessed is the Name of the Majestic Lord
passages.tafsir:
This single ayah is the seal of Sūrah ar-Raḥmān. The sūrah, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, is replete with verses calling attention to Allah's blessings, boons, and bounties, and His favours upon man — most recently the two further gardens with their gushing springs, their fruits, date palms and pomegranates, and the companions of Paradise. Now the sūrah closes by turning the reader's gaze from the gifts back to the Giver: *"Blessed is the Name of your Lord, full of Majesty and Honour."*

## The synopsis of the whole sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why this verse stands where it does: since Sūrah ar-Raḥmān is filled with verses that call attention to Allah's blessings and bounties, this ayah has been appended as a **synopsis** of them all. Its logic is striking: what can one say about the Pure Being Himself, when *even His Name* is glorious? All the divine boons and bounties the sūrah has just paraded before us subsist by virtue of His Name. The sūrah that asked, again and again, "Then which of the blessings of your Lord will you both deny?" ends by naming the source of every one of those blessings and declaring it *blessed* (tabāraka).

## Dhul-Jalāl wal-Ikrām — Majesty and Honour

The ayah closes on a compound title of Allah: **Dhul-Jalāl wal-Ikrām**, "the Owner of Majesty and Honour." Ibn Kathir reports the explanation of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās: it means *the Owner of greatness and pride* — greatness and glory belong to Allah alone.

Ibn Kathir then draws out what this title demands of us. Because Allah is Dhul-Jalāl wal-Ikrām, He is:

- **worthy of being honoured** — and so always obeyed;
- **worthy of being revered** — and thus worshipped;
- **worthy of being appreciated** — and never unappreciated;
- **worthy of being remembered** — and never forgotten.

Notice how each attribute pairs with a duty. Majesty calls for obedience; honour calls for worship; blessing calls for gratitude; and the One whose very Name is blessed must never slip from our remembrance. This is the fitting close to a sūrah built around that recurring challenge to stop denying His favours: the only sane response to such a Lord is honour, worship, thanks, and remembrance.

## From the Sunnah: living under this Name

Ibn Kathir gathers several teachings of the Prophet ﷺ around this ayah, and together they show that Dhul-Jalāl wal-Ikrām is not merely a phrase to admire but a Name to *use*.

**A duʿā to hold onto.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Rabīʿah bin ʿĀmir said that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: *"Persist (in invoking Allah) with, 'Yā Dhal-Jalāl wal-Ikrām' (O Owner of greatness and honour)."* An-Nasa'i also collected this hadith. The instruction is to be *persistent* — to make this Name a constant refrain in one's supplication, clinging to it the way the sūrah itself keeps returning to its refrain.

**After every prayer.** Muslim and the Four Sunan compilers recorded from ʿĀ'ishah that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ finished his prayer with the salām, he would sit only as long as it took him to say: *"O Allah! You are As-Salām, and peace comes from You. Blessed be You, Yā Dhal-Jalāl wal-Ikrām."* Notice that this remembrance echoes the ayah's own wording — *tabārakta*, "Blessed be You" — addressed to the Owner of Majesty and Honour. At the close of every prayer, the believer repeats in miniature what this ayah does at the close of the sūrah.

**Honouring what Allah has honoured.** Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ taught that among the acts of venerating Allah are honouring the elderly Muslim, the one in authority, and the carrier (memorizer) of the Qur'an who avoids extremism and laziness with it. Reverence for the Lord of Majesty and Honour is proven not only on the tongue but in how we treat grey-haired believers, legitimate authority, and the people of the Qur'an.

## Living it

The believer who reaches the end of Sūrah ar-Raḥmān should carry three things away from this closing verse. First, gratitude with a direction: every blessing counted in the sūrah traces back to one blessed Name, so thank the Named, not merely the gifts. Second, a phrase for the tongue: "Yā Dhal-Jalāl wal-Ikrām" in supplication, and "Allāhumma anta as-Salām..." after each prayer, exactly as the Prophet ﷺ practised. Third, a manner of life: veneration of Allah shown in honouring those He has dignified — the elderly Muslim, the upright authority, the bearer of His Book.

Ibn Kathir ends his commentary on the sūrah here with words that suit the ayah perfectly: all praise is due to Allah, and all favours come from Him.
